transcript.line: Sure! I was born and raised in Belgrade, Serbia, where I completed my bachelor’s and master’s studies in electrical engineering, focusing on signals and systems. This was my first exposure to machine learning theory.

After gaining some work experience there, I moved to Belgium to pursue a PhD in bioengineering. It might sound like a strange switch, but the theory of systems modeling applies across domains. Many data scientists switch fields because the underlying principles are universal.

However, I quickly realized academia wasn’t for me. After a year and a half, I accepted an offer from Deloitte Consulting in Belgium, where I worked for about three years. My PhD was my first paid job in data science, and at Deloitte, I started doing more machine learning engineering, including prototyping models and deploying them.

Back then, MLOps wasn’t a term, but someone had to do it. I learned proper Python development practices, project packaging, and deploying on AWS. By 2019, I was fully focused on machine learning engineering.

Over the last five to six years, I’ve worked mainly in the financial industry, which is why we had our previous talk. I’ve worked with several big banks, including ING, BNP Paribas, Euroclear, and KBC.

In June last year, I decided to become a freelancer, something I’d planned for years. I took a short mission with KBC and then joined a Brussels-based startup called Tempo, where I helped industrialize some Python code. Starting February, I’ll be working with another company in Ghent.

I’ve worked across various industries, including healthcare, transportation, logistics, and chemicals. Most of my experience has been with Fortune 500 companies, but working with a startup has been an eye-opening experience.

transcript.header: Startup Pace: Agility, Speed, and Managerial Insights

transcript.line: Working in a startup feels like flying. You don’t have the bureaucratic restrictions that exist in big corporations. Of course, those restrictions often serve as safety nets, but they can also slow things down.

The last two months have made me want to go back to my previous companies and ask, “Why can’t we move at least half as fast?” I think many managers in traditional corporations could benefit from spending time in a startup to see how agile and fast-paced things can be.

transcript.header: Lean MLOps: Shoestring Strategies for Early-Stage Companies

transcript.line: When we met at the DataMakers Fest conference, we ended up in the same car and started talking. I also attended your talk, which was about doing MLOps on a shoestring budget.

The main idea was that you don’t need fancy tools to get started with MLOps. You showed how to use basic tools and principles to get going. It felt very startup-like—starting simple and adding complexity as needed, versus the corporate approach of planning everything in advance.
How well do those ideas translate to the startup world?

They translate very well. Startups have to be lean because they often operate on tight budgets. When I delivered that talk, one of the first slides clarified what “shoestring” can mean. We usually think of it as a tight budget, which is true for startups.

Some startups might raise significant funding, like $500 million, to develop advanced AI, but that’s not the norm. Some startups have tight budgets in terms of money, while others are constrained by time or human resources.

In big companies, there’s usually more money, but you need to choose your battles carefully. It’s like having a gun with six bullets—you need to aim and shoot carefully. That’s the shoestring in a corporation.

In a startup, it’s usually about money and the number of people. Decisions like hiring or adopting new tools require careful consideration. It’s tempting in startups to use many tools because it’s easy to make quick agreements.

In a startup, you can just talk to one or two people and make a decision. This can lead to an explosion of tools and accounts, which is something big corporations prevent. In a corporation, you’re told, “This is the way we do it. End of story.”

For example, in my previous company, onboarding a new vendor was an adventure. It involved so many people, and the contract wasn’t even large. The next time I needed to onboard a new tool, I’d think twice.
In a startup, it’s different. You might sit next to someone and say, “Hey, I just saw this demo. How about we try it?” And the answer is, “Yeah, let’s try it.” That’s exactly how it goes.

transcript.header: SaaS-First Approach: Vendor Solutions for Small Teams

transcript.line: At Tempo, where I’m working now, it’s like, “Should we try this? Should we try that? Let’s try Logfire, Grafana, or this other tool.” You experiment and keep what works best.

I think startups should go for vendor solutions, like cloud-based software-as-a-service (SaaS), instead of building their own. Big companies often want to build their own solutions, but that requires maintenance.
When you have four to ten people in a company, you don’t want a dedicated person for BI or infrastructure. You’d rather use SaaS and avoid hiring someone to maintain servers.

transcript.header: Cloud Trade-offs: Startup Credits, Migration Friction, and Lock-in

transcript.line: Going on-premise is hard for a startup unless it makes a lot of sense. I think it’s a no-brainer for startups to go for the cloud. However, there needs to be a clever decision because migrating from one cloud to another can be slow and annoying.

Google, for example, has a “catch them while they’re young” program. They offer credits to get startups to use their platform. Many companies take the offer, and some stay even if they’re not entirely happy because migrating is costly.
It’s a strategy. Last time I checked, Google offered significant credits to small businesses—maybe around $50,000. For a small company, that could mean free cloud usage for a year.
But there’s a catch. You have to stay within Google Cloud, and some services might not be included. It’s a bit of a trick. If you burn through the credits in a month, that’s your problem.
Can’t it become chaotic? It’s so easy to start using a new tool, and then you end up with a bunch of tools that barely connect, and everything falls apart.

transcript.header: Cloud Complexity: Infrastructure as Code and Operational Overhead

transcript.line: Yes, the cloud adds extra complexity. I’ve worked mainly on-premise for about seven to eight years out of my ten years in data science. I always wanted more cloud experience, but when I fully switched to the cloud, I thought, “Wait, I want to go back to on-premise.”

On-premise has its limitations. It’s less flexible, and scaling is a challenge. But in the end, the infrastructure is straightforward. You have machines—bare metal or virtual machines—switches, disks, and applications running behind firewalls.

In the cloud, you have key management, identity management, and so many moving parts to configure. It quickly becomes overwhelming. Without infrastructure as code, it’s a mess. Even with infrastructure as code, it’s manageable but still complex.

If you start configuring things manually, it’s hard to replicate later. For example, I once deployed something through the console due to time constraints. Six months later, I wondered if I could repeat it. Would I remember all the steps?

The cloud adds an extra layer of complexity. You might have one tool for dashboards, another for logging, and so on. There’s no analytical formula to optimize and find the perfect tool stack. It’s more of an NP-hard problem—you just have to make the best choice.

As I understand, you work with young companies—startups—that rely on the cloud. But most of your experience has been with big companies. Now, in the last two months, you’ve had to make choices for startups.

transcript.header: MVP Stack: Prioritizing Tools for Rapid Prototyping and Launch

transcript.line: Yes, for this startup, the priority was to have certain features ready within two months: a visualization dashboard, an industrialized API, and so on. The goal was to make it robust and fast so we could move to the next stage and launch the product.

Based on experience, I can’t justify trying 20 different tools. Instead, I say, “Based on my experience, this is a good choice. Let’s go with it.” If it takes a day or two to prototype, I show it and ask, “Does this look good? Let’s go with that.”
You can’t go wrong with certain tools. For example, if you choose PostgreSQL as your database, no one will question it. It’s a proven choice.

At the beginning, you might not need complex tools. For example, we recently discussed Kubeflow in Slack. Kubeflow is a full-blown Kubernetes-based MLOps platform. I’ve never tried it, but I’ve seen demos. It seems like a huge pain with all the YAML files and Kubernetes complexity.

transcript.header: Portability vs Managed Services: Avoiding Vendor Lock-In (Vertex AI, SageMaker)

transcript.line: I tried Kubeflow, and it was a huge pain because of all the YAML files and Kubernetes complexity. Maybe it makes sense in the long run, but at the beginning, you might just need Flask or something simpler.

In your talk, you showed how to get started with simple tools instead of going for big solutions that you might need in two years. Right now, the goal is to move quickly and choose the simplest tool for the task.
The idea is to make sure it’s fast, reliable, and not overly complicated so you can move quickly. If you need to spend a week configuring Kubeflow, maybe it’s not the best tool for now.
The richer a solution is in features, the more it locks you in. For example, if you’re doing something in Python with scripts on a remote server, you can always change the server or provider.

But if you’re using something like Google Cloud’s Vertex AI or AWS SageMaker, you’re pretty much tied to that platform. If you want to migrate later, you’ll need to retrain models. The question is, were those models trained in a reproducible way?
So, the takeaway is to make your choices as portable as possible at the beginning. Choose tools that are more generic rather than specific to a particular vendor.

transcript.header: Low-Code Trade-offs: Speed vs Future Flexibility

transcript.line: Yes, that makes you more portable. Some startups might want to start as fast as possible using low-code solutions. If you can only hire a data scientist and not a proper software or systems engineer, you might go with a low-code platform.
In that case, the data scientist develops a model in a notebook environment and deploys it with a click. That can work, but I prefer having the freedom to avoid lock-in.

transcript.header: Career Decision Framework: Choosing Startups or Corporations

transcript.line: Let’s imagine I am a machine learning engineer with two offers—one from a startup and one from a Fortune 500 company. How should I decide between the two?
Let’s say the startup pays less but offers some stock options. For this scenario, imagine our engineer doesn’t need to prioritize money heavily.
It depends on several factors. Personally, I would lean toward a startup, especially depending on the stage of your career. Are we talking about someone in the early stages of their career?
Maybe we can explore what factors we should consider in making this decision.

In a corporation, you typically have job security and a narrow scope of work. If you’re fine specializing in one area, sticking to it, and working a predictable 9-to-5 schedule, then a corporation might be the right choice. This is a legitimate decision, and I followed it for many years.
On the other hand, if you want to move faster, learn quicker, and try out more things without spending unnecessary time in meetings, a startup is a better fit. However, startups come with risks.

For instance, if the atmosphere in a small company is bad, there’s no escaping it. In a larger company, you have the option to switch teams or departments, which provides some flexibility. Large corporations also offer internal mobility, letting you shift between data engineering, machine learning, MLOps, DevOps, and so on.

In startups, if things go south, the impact is more immediate. However, in the right startup environment—like the one I’m in now—it can be incredibly rewarding. That said, I’ve heard stories of less ideal startup experiences.

Startups often involve working toward future gains, like the eventual sale of the company. For someone early in their career, wanting to learn a lot, I also recommend consultancies. Like startups, consultancies expose you to various tools and approaches, allowing you to triangulate patterns and identify best practices.

In large companies, there’s often a rigid approach to processes. For example, I’ve seen CICD pipelines or Python projects set up in ways that were clearly wrong, but employees had adapted to them. Sometimes, they didn’t even realize these setups were suboptimal.
When I pointed out issues to one company, a team member told me she always felt something was wrong but lacked the arguments to explain why.
Even if something is wrong in a corporation, you don’t always have the flexibility to change it.

Exactly. If you’ve only ever seen one way of doing things, it’s hard to imagine alternatives. You might feel something is off but lack the knowledge to propose a better solution. That’s where external experience can help. Someone from outside can show a better approach.

If you graduate, join a corporation, and stay there for ten years, you only know one way of doing things. It might not be the best way, but it’s all you’ve learned. In a startup, you explore multiple approaches, gaining broader exposure.

transcript.header: End-to-End Ownership: Multidisciplinary Work in Startups

transcript.line: Startups also pivot frequently. A small, young startup might shift directions completely based on client demands. One client might leave, and another might request something entirely different. This kind of abrupt change keeps things exciting but also challenging.
For me, startups feel like a pack of hunters navigating the wild, chasing something big and uncertain. There’s a strong sense of camaraderie and ownership.

In the last two months at Tempo, I’ve done work that would require two or three separate teams in a large corporation. Beyond my core tasks—industrializing Python code—I provisioned infrastructure, created pipelines, and managed repositories on my own.

In many big companies, you can’t even create a repository without submitting a ticket. It feels bureaucratic, like waiting in line at city hall. You know how to do the task, but the system won’t let you.

transcript.header: Corporate Processes: "Agile" vs Bureaucratic Planning Cycles

transcript.line: Big corporations often label their processes as "agile," but it’s often just waterfall broken into smaller increments. For example, if you miss a quarterly planning session, you’re told to wait three months for the next one.
I have PTSD; you have flashbacks. Flashbacks now? Oh, sorry, it’s not for this quarter.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. No, but—how should I say—I said in advance I’m going to bash corporations a bit, but I had a lot of good times there. I had a lot of very good teams, very good friends, which I really love.
And, yeah, these corporations, as I said, they give you some stability. They give you some... I would say you know what to expect there. And you learn some things, also.

For example, this whole networking thing in a big company—it’s even more important than your hands-on knowledge. It’s about building a network within the company and having, what I would call, “my guy” in DevOps or “my guy” in networking.

You have people with whom you have good connections. It shouldn’t be like that because everything should work through requests and processes, but in the end, you know that out of ten people, there’s this one person you know, and they’ll get things done faster for you.
So yeah, again, it’s like a city hall: if you know the right people.

I summarize what you said. In a corporation, you get stability, financial safety, and a narrow scope of work. You become a specialist in one thing. Plus, there’s some guidance and framework, which, if you’re just starting, can teach you how to do things.

You also have internal mobility. But there’s less flexibility in technology because many decisions have already been made. It can feel like a city hall or town hall because there are so many different teams.

To get something done, you often need to create tickets, which adds bureaucratic overhead. As you mentioned, there’s quarterly planning, and if something isn’t planned for this quarter, you may have to wait for the next.

In startups, you move and learn faster. There are fewer meetings and less bureaucracy. You work with greenfield projects without legacy frameworks or structures. While frameworks can be helpful, they can also slow you down.
But wait, a good framework should make you move faster. In a corporation, one of my roles was creating frameworks to speed things up.

For example, if we knew that over the next two or three years we’d have similar projects—like building models for email classification and deploying them—then we’d create templates to make deployments faster.

transcript.header: Platform & Frameworks: Automating Developer Workflows

transcript.line: That’s how it should work. But something goes wrong when companies slice and dice domains of responsibility too much.

Ideally, developers or application builders shouldn’t even know a DevOps or platform team exists. They should have everything automated and ready to go, only needing to submit a few initial requests to set up infrastructure.
Of course, nobody should be able to spin up 100 VMs with 100 GPUs unchecked, but the process can be streamlined.
These downsides aren’t inevitable in corporations. They have the resources and people to do better.

transcript.header: Team Scale Advantages: Redundancy, Support, and Internal Mobility

transcript.line: One advantage in corporations is being part of a big team. If you go on holiday, someone else can pick up your work. In startups, this is much harder because they’re so lean.
In a corporation, there’s always someone to help you troubleshoot or answer questions. In a startup, it’s more chaotic.
There’s a general rule: don’t be the first data scientist in an organization if you’re a junior. It’s fine if you’re senior, but if you’re the only person, look somewhere else.
So what you’re saying is that startups have more chaos, and you need to be comfortable with it.
Exactly. It’s like a warpath. You need to be robust. It’s never boring, though!

transcript.header: Startup Intensity: Learning Curve, Burnout Risk, and Rewards

transcript.line: But also, what you didn’t mention—and what I experienced—is that it’s never boring. Yes, and you have this cool end-to-end ownership of things.
You feel this: "Okay, I produce some code, and I see it in action." It doesn’t need to go through ten steps of approval or whatever.
But on the other hand, because of the constant firefighting mode—constantly pivoting, constantly working on something—things break, and you try to fix them.
At least, that was my experience. At the end of the day, I felt exhausted. I gave more than 100%, and it was super difficult for me to do anything after work.
After one year, I was like, "I’m burned out." In corporations, that doesn’t happen.
You don’t have to move at that speed. In startups, you’re running all the time, whereas in a corporation, it’s more like a walk in the park.
Yeah, but that’s what I’m saying. Both have their pluses and minuses.
For me, it’s refreshing that I can move at my maximum speed. But again, I’ve only been doing this for two months.
If I kept this pace for a year, I’d probably also be close to burnout. But, you know, in Eastern Europe, we don’t have burnout.
Right? What is that?
We don’t accept it.
But the amount of things I learned—because I needed to build so many things from scratch and solve real problems with real clients—was incredible.
Yeah, that’s true.

transcript.header: AI-Assisted Coding: Productivity Gains and Technical Debt Risks

transcript.line: But you know what I see as a risk now with LLMs and AI-assisted coding?
It’s a kind of trap. I realized how quickly I could do many things for which I’m not really an expert, and it works.
But I’m thinking, okay, this has only been two months. What if I work like this for two years?
My primary competence is Python, but suddenly, I’m doing Ansible scripts, GitHub pipelines, and HTML with AI's help.
AI helps me so much that I can handle 10–20 different areas. But what happens when this code needs to be maintained?
Because I’ve seen people online bragging about how one person can do three weeks’ work alone. But how much of that code is technical debt?
What part of the code will become a monster to maintain a year later?
Ninety percent of it, probably.
Exactly. That’s why I joke that we had "schema-on-write" with SQL, then "schema-on-read" with NoSQL.
Now, with AI coding, it’s "learn-on-write" and later "learn-on-maintain."
When the code breaks, you have to go back and learn it all over again.
It’s going to make things very interesting.
For a startup, it might be okay, depending on how much technical debt you let accumulate.
Yeah, but imagine you see some weird code in a company. You run git blame and ask, "Who wrote this?"
Often, I ask, "Why did you do this exception handling in this way?" And the person explains the reasoning.
What if that person is you?

transcript.header: Technical Debt Management: Notes, Awareness, and Security Implications

transcript.line: Yeah, that also happens. But I think LLMs are drastically increasing the amount of technical debt we’re creating.
You can move fast. I’ve done certain simple applications super quickly.
But for a startup, isn’t it okay to move fast and deal with technical debt later?
Of course, you need to keep in mind that you’ll have to repay this debt, but you accept it.
Yes, but someone needs to be aware of the risks.
Whenever I do something quick and dirty, I leave a note saying, “This needs to be checked.”
But if you’re a junior, you might not be aware of what you’re leaving behind.
It’s easy to move fast and leave ports open or create security holes.
For example, if your startup’s value is 90% in its data and that data gets leaked, you’ve killed your startup.
Moving fast is fine if you take informed risks. You need to have a strategy and be aware of vulnerabilities you’re living with.
If you rely on LLMs without much thought, you’re risking a lot.
So, be ready to repay that debt at some point.
Yes, it’s like a loan—you use it to leverage something and deliver value quickly, but you need to be aware of repayment.
That’s why it’s not a good idea for a junior to join a startup as the only data scientist.
With LLMs, juniors can do a lot, but their lack of experience means they might not realize what’s suboptimal.
Without someone to guide them, it can create big problems.

transcript.header: Early-Career Advice: Mentorship, Pairing, and Role Selection

transcript.line: For juniors, is it better to join a corporation or a more established company?
Any company where there are at least two or more seniors to learn from is ideal.
As a junior, you’ll learn anywhere in your first 2–3 years, but after that, you might feel saturated.
In consulting, jumping from client to client is normal. But in other fields, jumping from job to job might look bad on your CV.

transcript.header: Minimal MLOps Stack: Python, CI/CD Orchestration, and Dagster

transcript.line: We have quite a few questions. One is: What tools do you use for your MLOps projects, and how do you balance time between new and old tools?
Right now, my approach is to keep things as minimal as possible.
I mainly use Python for scripts and training, and I try to handle orchestration through CI/CD pipelines.
I’m starting a project with Dagster for orchestration, which I’m excited about.
You need some kind of orchestrator. I’ve used MLflow and recently helped a startup set up their internal MLflow tracking server.
For MLOps frameworks, there aren’t many components: model registries, feature stores, etc.
I haven’t set up a feature store yet but try to pick top tools that are mature and established.

transcript.header: Observability Choices: Logfire, Prometheus/Grafana, and Streamlit

transcript.line: For observability, I recently used Logfire, which I really liked.
Logfire is from the creator of Pydantic. It sends detailed logs and tracebacks with minimal setup.
Compared to something like Grafana and Prometheus, Logfire was working within an hour.
It collects application logs, system logs, memory, and CPU usage.
It also has plugins for frameworks like FastAPI and TensorFlow, which add extra functionality.
There are lots of options out there, and many blog posts cover possible configurations.
Yeah, so I think, yeah, that sounds—it's the first time I hear about this. So previously, like for logs, the tool I would go with would be ELK: Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana.
Or sometimes instead of Logstash, you have something else, but it's not Point B.
It's very new. It's like less than a year old, and it's like the big, big new project from the Pantic people.
When it comes to Grafana, you don't use it usually?
No, I started and I gave up. It looks like too mature, so I'm not a BI person. And, for example, yeah, recently I used Streamlit for some visualization.

I really like how Streamlit works. Of course, it's so simple. It's so simple, but the only thing I have a problem with—like also MLflow and Streamlit—is the moment you want to get to the point of authentication.
Like, they do have some basic authentication, but it's hard to get like full enterprise-level stuff, you know.
Like, I don't know, integrating with Active Directory or whatnot. For that, you need to take some kind of a paid version.
Databricks has it or whatever, yeah.

transcript.header: Product Modularity: Desire for Standalone Model Registries & Observability

transcript.line: Yeah, it's not that simple. I remember trying to talk to Databricks people, saying, "Hey, I just want MLflow with authentication. I don’t need anything else, just MLflow."
Yeah, but, you know, it only comes with the Databricks platform, so you kind of have to take the whole thing.
Yeah, yeah, that's also, I think, a bad decision. If any vendors are listening, I think every product should be as modular as possible.
And that you can just take that part, you know. If you have like a really good model registry, you should let people use just your model registry.
Or just very good observability, just let people use that one and don't force them to buy everything.
Maybe Databricks doesn’t really care about MLflow that much. They care more about selling because this is where they make money.
And people eventually just go with Weights & Biases or something like that for their registry or whatever.

transcript.header: Skill Investment: Foundational Tools (Linux, Python, Bash) vs New Tech

transcript.line: Like, this question actually has three questions. So, the second one is: what's your advice on investing time in new or old tools?
I guess the question is like: how do you, um, well, balance between old and new tools?
Yeah, well, I would say the old tools are the ones that have survived everything—the every apocalypse.
You should definitely always learn about them. I would say Linux, you should know Linux, Python—these things are foundational.
Bash scripting, if you know these things. A bit of networking, a bit of Ansible or some of these tools are very, very useful.
A bit of frontend development, just to know how HTML, CSS, and JavaScript work together to make a very simple application.
All these things give you a lot of depth.
Maybe you shouldn't go with Java 6, right?
I also don't think that. There are people who are still—there are young people learning mainframe development, you know.
And you still have a lot of mainframe code. So, it's like a gamble. What's your risk appetite?
Do you want to target a certain niche? Yeah, you can learn probably HLL or Perl and find a job with it.
And there will not be a big pool of candidates for that. But then, you have to be ready to be hungry for a couple of months potentially while waiting for the right job.
But if you're still coding and you're hungry, it's worth it, right?
But, if you want to play it safe, it's very simple. You open up job postings, make a little scraping script, download a lot of job postings, and see what the repeated keywords are.
And you learn those. That’s basically what I did. That’s how I got into Python.

transcript.header: Market Signals for Learning: Job Postings, Airflow, and Targeted Skills

transcript.line: Yeah, and if you do that and see that all companies use Airflow, and that’s all they want...
But Airflow is okay—it works, but not the best user experience. There are so many other orchestrators.
Even though 70% of companies still stick to Airflow, I understand why most banks still stick to Java, right?
Even though there are other languages. So, in this case, I do the scraping. I see these are the tools: Java, Airflow. How do I try to include new things here that not all use?
I would say, from time to time, you need to tick some boxes. That’s what I did with Azure.
Although I’m not currently working on Azure, I got feedback from recruiters that in Belgium, a lot of companies are using Azure.
So, it’s very good to have a certain certification. So, I thought, okay, I’ll get a certification in Azure.
I would say, do at least the bare minimum to understand a tool. You don’t have to become an expert in Airflow.
How much time does it take to know something about it? A couple of days of playing with it.
Then you can say, “I know something.” You can do a course and check the box.
For example, with PySpark, four out of five interviews I had asked me about PySpark.
They even had Spark clusters—though not always. Two out of five times, they had Spark clusters.
But I never spent more than 1% of my time doing anything with Spark.
But it’s like, “Do you have the box?” You said yes, and it’s not important, but it’s still part of the process.

transcript.header: Data Engineering Reliability: Quality, Lineage, and LLM Unpredictability

transcript.line: I think it’s similar with people in AI. Data engineering is much older than MLOps engineering, and still, you hear many senior data engineers saying, "Hey, we’re still facing the same issues with data quality, lineage, and so on." So yeah, we’re not a fad anymore; we’re not the popular kids. But there’s still work to do.

When I transitioned into machine learning engineering—originally, I was a data scientist—my goal was to build tools for the data scientist I used to be. I wanted to create something that would make my former self’s life easier. But even today, I haven’t seen companies make that experience seamless.

There’s still so much left to do. With LLMs, the challenges are even more complicated. For example, you can hijack many chatbots to write code or do things they weren’t intended for. You might start on an e-commerce site and suddenly manipulate it into doing something else if you’re clever enough.

And to be honest, the fact that I can’t fully rely on LLMs for validation makes me hesitant to use them at all. It feels too unpredictable. As an engineer, I want systems to be predictable, work 100% of the time, and be repeatable unless someone pulls the plug on a server. Having to wonder whether an LLM might hallucinate and return YAML instead of JSON? Call me back when that’s sorted out.
That’s interesting because machine learning, in general, isn’t deterministic either. But at least we’ve learned to make it reliable, right? As ML engineers, we’re still figuring that out with LLMs.

Yeah, exactly. At least with classical machine learning, the output is structured in a predictable way, and I can control it. But with LLMs, sometimes it feels like you’re just begging—like, "Please, just give me a valid response. My career depends on it!" There’s even a meme about that.

transcript.header: On-Premise vs Cloud: Privacy, Cost Efficiency, and Migration Strategy

transcript.line: Right. So maybe let’s take one last question. You mentioned you have experience with on-premise systems. Most corporations you’ve worked with have preferred on-premise over cloud solutions. Luka is asking: Do you think on-premise will be the future for companies that care about data privacy? Especially in fields like finance or healthcare, where data privacy is critical.

Yes, absolutely. That’s one of the main reasons companies are hesitant to fully embrace the cloud. In the financial industry, for example, most companies are still on-premise but are gradually moving to the cloud. However, they’re very cautious about what they migrate.
Technically, these migrations could be done in a few months, but they often take years because of necessary discussions around privacy, encryption, and security risks like man-in-the-middle attacks.

That said, there’s been a trend in recent years of companies moving back to on-premise. If you have a skilled team of engineers, you can save millions. For instance, the creator of Ruby on Rails, DHH, has written about how his company moved back to on-premise and drastically reduced costs.

Right. AWS Lambda, for example, is great when you’re just starting out and don’t have a predictable workload. But once your workload stabilizes, it makes sense to switch to dedicated machines that are always running. It’s the same with cloud versus on-premise. At some point, you realize it’s cheaper in the long run to manage it yourself.
Exactly. But to do that, you need the right expertise. A data scientist using a low-code platform probably won’t have the skills to manage an on-premise setup.

Alright, one quick question to wrap up. We talked about Spark earlier, and you mentioned you didn’t have to use it extensively, but it’s often a key topic in interviews. Have you used Dask? Do you think it’s a good alternative for distributed training?

I’ve experimented with Dask, but only locally. Once, I had some parallel processing to do and tried chunking a big DataFrame with Dask. But for some reason, it ended up being slower than just using Pandas.

That might have been due to how I used it. Performance depends on what you’re doing—whether you’re aggregating, merging, or something else. For aggregations, Dask might be faster. But for smaller operations like merging, performance can tank.

I’ve written about this before, comparing tools like Spark and Ray. With distributed systems, if you’re just doing a group-by and aggregate, it’s fine. But when you start merging small tables across clusters, it can become a disaster.

transcript.header: Distributed Compute Alternatives: Dask, Spark, and Performance Trade-offs

transcript.line: Dask is a mature tool, and I know it works in a distributed manner like Spark. However, I haven’t seen it widely used in the industry. Companies usually default to Spark for distributed processing. My limited success with Dask doesn’t mean it’s bad—just that I didn’t know how to use it properly.
That aligns with my experience. About five years ago, Dask couldn’t handle group-by operations well, but I think it’s improved since then.

transcript.header: Closing Remarks and Next Steps

transcript.line: Anyway, thanks so much for your time. This was an amazing discussion. It’s always a pleasure to have you as a guest. Maybe we can make this a recurring thing?
I’d love that. It’s always great chatting with you.
Thanks again, and thanks to everyone who joined us. I hope you enjoyed it. See you next time!
Bye, everyone!

description: Master Iceberg, Delta Lake and AI-powered pipelines to build scalable, governed data lakehouses—optimize ETL, boost real-time analytics and ML performance.
short: Trends in Data Engineering
title: Modern Data Engineering: Iceberg, Delta Lake & AI-Powered Pipelines

transcript.header: Episode opening & guest introduction

transcript.line: This week, we’ll talk about trends in data engineering. Our special guest today is Adrian, a returning guest. This is his third time on the podcast, but he’s also been part of workshops and open-source demos. Many of you probably know him already.

Adrian is the co-founder of DLT Hub, the company behind DLT, which we’ll discuss today. We’ll also talk about trends in data engineering. When we launched our Data Engineering Zoom Camp recently, one of the questions from participants was, “How do you see data engineering evolving, and what are the trends?” I realized I couldn’t answer that, so I thought of Adrian.
Welcome to the podcast, Adrian. It’s a pleasure to have you here again.

transcript.header: Perspective on evolving data engineering challenges

transcript.line: The pleasure is mine. I don’t have all the answers, but I can share my perspective and observations.
That’s what makes it interesting. Everyone has opinions, and you’re much closer to data engineering than I am.
As always, the questions for today’s interview were prepared by Johanna Bayer. Thank you, Johanna, for your help.
Before we dive into trends, let’s start with your background. Can you briefly share your career journey?

transcript.header: Career journey: startups, freelancing, founding DLT

transcript.line: Sure. I started in data in 2012. I spent five years working at startups in Berlin, building data warehouses. Then I joined an enterprise but didn’t enjoy it, so I became a freelancer for five years.
After freelancing, I wanted to do more than just consulting. I didn’t enjoy managing an agency, so I decided to build DLT, a tool I wish I had as a data engineer. That’s the short version.
You mentioned DLT is a tool you wish you had as a data engineer. Do you use it often?

transcript.header: DLT as a Python-based ingestion standard and market impact

transcript.line: I use it all the time. As a data engineer, much of your work involves data ingestion—taking data from semi-structured formats like JSON and transforming it into a structured format. DLT automates this process, so there’s no reason to use anything else.
Do you remember when we last spoke on the podcast?
Just over a year ago, I think.
Yes, over a year ago. You were already at DLT, and we talked about your journey from freelancing to founding a company.
Since then, a lot has changed. I’ve enjoyed visiting your office and seeing your team grow. You’ve moved to a bigger space, and it’s been amazing to witness your progress.
From an outsider’s perspective, it’s been exciting. Can you share what’s been happening internally over the past year?
We started by squatting in other people’s offices, but now we’ve grown significantly. Last year, I talked about creating a standard for data ingestion with DLT, and I think we’ve succeeded.

DLT has become a standard for Python-based data ingestion. We’ve commoditized this market, making it accessible to everyone. This has challenged the industry to offer more value beyond just connectors.
Are you still actively working as a data engineer, or what does your role look like now?

transcript.header: DLT Plus vision and partnership outreach for freelancers

transcript.line: Right now, I’m focused on DLT Plus, figuring out how to make it a meaningful product. We’re building a data platform around DLT, incorporating best practices and innovation.
So your work involves figuring out how DLT Plus will function?
Yes, as a founder, my role involves exploring initiatives, listening to feedback, and testing ideas. I’m also working on building a partnership network to maximize value for customers.
For freelancers listening, how can they reach out to learn more about this partnership network?
They can reach out on LinkedIn or find partnership links on our website. This is mainly for people already using DLT.
You’ve been in the data engineering industry for over a decade. How has the industry changed over the past five years?

transcript.header: Industry shift toward specialization: governance, data quality, streaming

transcript.line: Five years ago, there was a shortage of data engineers, and anyone who could do basic integration was called a data engineer. Now, the field is becoming more specialized.

We’re seeing data engineers focus on areas like data governance, data quality, and streaming. These specializations often have little overlap, driven by industry requirements like handling sensitive data or new use cases like energy management.
For junior data engineers, is it harder to enter the field now?

transcript.header: Early-career opportunities: AI projects and startup hiring

transcript.line: It depends. There’s still opportunity, especially in AI. Many companies are exploring AI and need data engineers to support those efforts. Startups also need help building modern data stacks, which has become easier with tools like DLT.
You mentioned the modern data stack. How modern is it, and what does it entail?

transcript.header: Modern data stack critique and open-source "postmodern" alternatives

transcript.line: The modern data stack is largely marketing. It’s a package of software from various vendors that you can combine to build a data platform.
For example, Fivetran with Snowflake and Looker. Vendors needed a way to sell together, and the modern data stack concept was born. It’s effective marketing, but not necessarily modern.
Now, people are talking about the postmodern data stack, which uses open-source technologies to achieve better efficiency and lower costs.
Fivetran, Snowflake, and Looker aren’t open source, right?
Correct, but you can build similar stacks with open-source tools.
What trends do you think we’ll see more of in 2025 and beyond?

transcript.header: 2025 trends: AI integration in data engineering and Apache Iceberg adoption

transcript.line: AI will continue to grow, with more complex use cases and fewer hallucinations. AI is entering the data engineering space, with data engineers building AI agents.
Another trend is Apache Iceberg. It’s moving from hype to production deployments, especially with Pythonic implementations.
Can you explain what Apache Iceberg is?

transcript.header: Apache Iceberg explained: table format, Parquet storage, vendor lock-in reduction

transcript.line: Iceberg is a table format that simulates the storage layer of a SQL database. It’s a way of storing data independently of databases, allowing updates without rewriting entire files.
So it’s a bunch of Parquet files on S3 with metadata?
Yes, it’s similar to Delta and Hudi. The industry is excited because it breaks vendor lock-in, but vendors are still trying to capture value through catalogs.
You mentioned databases have four layers: storage, compute, access, and metadata. Can you clarify what a catalog is?

transcript.header: Database layers and catalog role: storage, compute, access, metadata & lineage

transcript.line: A catalog maps data to compute and manages access control. Some catalogs also handle metadata, like lineage, which helps track data usage.
What tools are used for catalogs?

transcript.header: Metadata and catalog tooling overview (AWS Glue and peers)

transcript.line: I don’t recall all the names, but tools like AWS Glue Catalog are examples.
What about DuckDB? Will we see more “on-laptop” data warehouses?

transcript.header: DuckDB impact: embeddable local OLAP and portable query engine

transcript.line: DuckDB is amazing and a key technology for us. It’s embeddable, meaning you can use it as a building block in your own product.
We use DuckDB in DLT to query data through a universal interface, whether it’s a file system, data lake, or SQL database.
Is DuckDB changing how we do data engineering?

transcript.header: Cost-efficient pipelines: DuckDB with GitHub Actions and headless table formats

transcript.line: Absolutely. People are challenging the high costs of vendor solutions. I’ve seen setups using DuckDB and GitHub Actions to run entire data stacks for cents per month.
So DuckDB allows us to process data locally and save results back to storage?
Yes, and because it’s portable, you can take advantage of cheaper compute options like GitHub Actions.
Is DuckDB related to headless table formats?
Yes, DuckDB provides a local access layer, which is useful for data pipelines.
You mentioned headless table formats with DLT. Is that where you’re heading?

transcript.header: Headless table formats and DLT support for Delta Lake and Iceberg

transcript.line: Yes, we’re already serving headless Delta Lake and working on similar solutions for Iceberg.
Instead of processing everything in Snowflake and paying a fortune.
Exactly.

transcript.header: dbt's influence on engineering workflows and alternatives like SQLMesh

transcript.line: How did dbt change data engineering?
dbt changed how people think about data engineering. It eliminated boilerplate code and improved project quality.
What about alternatives like SQLMesh?
Competition is healthy. dbt was first, but tools like SQLMesh are doubling down on what dbt core offered.
What about workflow orchestration? What should we use in 2025?

transcript.header: Workflow orchestration options in 2025: Airflow, Prefect, Dagster, GitHub Actions

transcript.line: It depends on your team. Airflow is a common choice, but tools like Prefect and Dagster are also popular. We often use GitHub Actions for its cost efficiency.
For simple workflows, GitHub Actions is sufficient?
Yes, it’s serverless and much cheaper than always-on orchestrators.
Let’s move to audience questions.
For someone pursuing multiple disciplines like data engineering, data science, and AI engineering, I recommend focusing on one area first.

transcript.header: AI engineering convergence: data engineers building AI agents

transcript.line: AI engineering often overlaps with data engineering, especially when building systems like chatbots.
AI requires data, algorithms, and semantics. Data engineers will play a key role in building AI agents.
With so many tools in data engineering, how should beginners choose what to learn?

transcript.header: Beginner roadmap: SQL, Python, capturing business requirements, building a portfolio

transcript.line: Focus on understanding the concepts and solving problems. Tools are secondary. Learn SQL, Python, and how to capture business requirements.
For building a portfolio, is it okay to pick any tool for each component?
Yes, but consider the end user. Tools like notebooks or dashboards should align with how your audience interacts with data.
So, try things and see what works.

transcript.header: Tool selection guidance and vendor caution for modern data stacks

transcript.line: Exactly. The modern data stack is interchangeable, but be cautious of vendors with questionable practices.
How challenging is it for a senior backend engineer to transition into data engineering?

transcript.header: Transition paths: senior backend engineers moving into data engineering

transcript.line: It’s relatively easy. The main gap is understanding the business case and requirements.
So, a senior backend engineer can transition into a senior data engineering role.
Yes, unless they’re aiming for something highly specialized.
If you want to position yourself as a Spark expert, it might take time, but solving data problems is more about engineering skills.
If you’re a junior claiming to be a Spark expert, I’d be skeptical.

transcript.header: Job market outlook: senior vs junior data engineering opportunities

transcript.line: What’s the job market like for data engineers?
For seniors, there’s no shortage of jobs. Juniors might need to explore related roles like BI or data science to get started.
What are Delta and Hudi?

transcript.header: Table format comparisons: Delta, Hudi, and Iceberg differences

transcript.line: They’re similar to Iceberg but differ in design and optimization. Delta is the most mature, while Hudi is more specialized.
Are these formats suitable for streaming

transcript.header: Streaming architectures and tools: micro-batching, Kafka, SQS, Flink

transcript.line: Yes, but streaming is often just micro-batching unless you have strict SLAs.
What tools are used for streaming?
Kafka and SQS are common buffers. Downstream, tools like Flink or DuckDB can process the data.
Will data engineering be automated by AI?

transcript.header: AI-driven commoditization and code generation in data engineering

transcript.line: AI is speeding up commoditization, making it easier to generate code. Data engineers will specialize further and build AI agents.
What’s the future of DLT?

transcript.header: DLT roadmap: DLT Plus and a marketplace for reusable data products

transcript.line: In one year, we’re focusing on DLT Plus, a portable data platform. In five years, we aim to create a marketplace for data products, enabling reuse across organizations.

transcript.header: Episode wrap-up and key takeaways

transcript.line: It’s been great talking to you, Adrian. Thanks for sharing your insights.
Thanks, Alexey. See you later.
Goodbye, everyone.

description: Discover Production ML, system design, and competition rigor from a Kaggle Grandmaster—practical deployment tactics, model scaling tips, and education strategies.
short: Competitive Machine Learning and Teaching
title: From Kaggle Grandmaster to Production ML: Competition Rigor, System Design & Large-Scale Education

transcript.header: Episode Start
Guest Introduction & Kaggle Grandmaster Credentials

transcript.line: This week, we’ll talk about competitive machine learning and teaching. Our special guest today is Alexander Guschin, a machine learning engineer with 10+ years of experience, a Kaggle Grandmaster ranked 5th globally, and a teacher to over 100,000 students. He leads data science and software engineering teams and contributes to open-source machine learning tools. Welcome, Alexander!
Hi, thank you for having me. It’s great to talk to you today.
I also want to thank Marina for helping us get in touch. I’ve been following your work for over 10 years, so it’s a great moment to finally talk to you.
The questions for today’s interview were prepared by Johanna Bayer. Thank you, Johanna, for your help.
Before we dive into teaching and competitive machine learning, let’s start with your background. Can you tell us about your career journey so far?

transcript.header: Early Industry Roles & Open-Source Contributions

transcript.line: Sure. My career started about 10 years ago when I was a student at a university in Moscow. I was looking for an opportunity to learn machine learning, which was a new and exciting field at the time. I found that opportunity on Kaggle.

After Kaggle, I moved to the industry. I worked as a data analyst at Avito, then as a data scientist at Yandex, handling ride-sharing services. Later, I worked at Mechanica AI, a startup focused on bringing machine learning to industrial enterprises. We even traveled to small cities in Siberia to find product engineers and see if they needed our machine learning solutions.

Eventually, I worked at Iterative.ai, a San Francisco-based startup that creates open-source tools for machine learning engineers and data scientists. After that, I moved back to Moscow to work at Central University, where I now focus on teaching.
Since you mentioned Iterative.ai, I want to thank them for supporting this community. Their support helped grow the community to where it is today.

transcript.header: MLEM Story & Tooling Anecdotes

transcript.line: Yes, I was part of the team. My friend Mikhail Sveshenkov gave a talk at one of your events about a tool we were building called MLEM.
MLEM? Is that the sound a cat makes?
Yeah, it’s based on an internet meme where a dog or cat sticks its tongue out. We were trying to be funny.
Are you still involved in open-source projects?
Not right now. I mostly worked on open-source tools while at Iterative.

You mentioned starting your career as a student 10 years ago with Kaggle. For me, Kaggle was also a gateway into data science. I thought I was good at machine learning, but my first Kaggle competition showed me how much I still had to learn.

transcript.header: Kaggle Beginnings & Local Community Influence

transcript.line: I started Kaggle while studying at university. I chose a machine learning lab for my bachelor’s thesis but quickly realized how challenging it was. I found Kaggle as a place to test my practical skills.

There was a strong Kaggle community in Moscow, with weekly sessions where people shared solutions and discussed ideas. I spent a lot of time on Kaggle, even skipping lectures to focus on competitions.
Skipping lectures? Did you get kicked out of university?
No, the educational system allowed me to skip most of the semester and focus on exams.

transcript.header: Balancing Competitions with University Studies

transcript.line: How did you balance Kaggle and university?
I spent a lot of time on Kaggle, but I managed to pass my exams. It was a year of intense focus before I got my first job.
In Germany, it’s similar—what matters is how well you pass the exams, not how much you study during the semester.
Yeah, the system is changing now, but back then, it worked for me.

transcript.header: Time Investment & Learning Curve on Competitions

transcript.line: You said the secret to success on Kaggle is putting in a lot of time. I can confirm that. In one competition, I spent 3 months working on it, putting in 5-10 hours per week. It was exhausting, but I learned a lot.

transcript.header: Kaggle for Skill Broadening, Domain Exposure & Interviews

transcript.line: Kaggle broadens your perspective on machine learning. You learn different domains, models, and frameworks, which is incredibly valuable when you start working in the industry.
How long did you compete on Kaggle?
About a year. After that, I got my first job and continued competing, but it became harder to balance.
Was your first job as a data analyst?
Yes, at Avito.
Kaggle helped me throughout my career. I worked on a competition about duplicate detection, and that experience was useful in my job at OLX, which was the parent company of Avito.
My first serious competition was on a platform called CrowdAnalytix. The training set was small, so it was more about luck than skill.
Kaggle solutions often involve complex stacking, which isn’t practical for production. But you still learn a lot from competing.
Yes, you learn to explore the data carefully, do EDA, and build robust validation strategies.

transcript.header: Competition Preparation: Iteration, Baselines & Infrastructure

transcript.line: Did you do anything special to prepare for competitions?
Iteration is key. The more competitions you solve, the easier it gets. For hackathons, it’s useful to set up infrastructure and create baselines in advance.
Do you still take part in hackathons?

transcript.header: Applying Competition Experience to Production ML

transcript.line: Not anymore. Now I’m usually on the organizing side.
How did Kaggle help you transition to the industry?
Kaggle broadened my perspective on machine learning. It helped me understand different domains and frameworks, which was valuable in job interviews.
Kaggle also taught me to spot data leaks, which is useful in production. Plus, it helped me build a public profile and connect with others in the community.
Do you think Kaggle is still useful for starting a data science career today?

transcript.header: Regional Differences in Kaggle’s Career Value

transcript.line: It depends on your location and opportunities. In places like Kazakhstan, where educational resources are limited, Kaggle is still valuable. But in the US or Europe, there are other ways to start a career.
In Eastern Europe, competitions like Kaggle are more popular, possibly because of the strong focus on mathematics in schools.
That could be a factor.
Should we do competitive machine learning alone or in teams?

transcript.header: Collaboration Strategies: Teamwork vs. Solo Competitions

transcript.line: It’s better to form a team or at least have a community to discuss ideas. Different people explore different solutions, which can lead to better results.
Teams can combine models through stacking, which is often more effective.
Yes, even without stacking, having multiple predictions can be beneficial.
I remember a competition where the winning team combined expertise in different areas.
Yes, they found a data leak, which was key to their success.
You teach school children about machine learning?

transcript.header: Teaching Teens & Participation in AI Olympiads

transcript.line: Yes, I teach 16-18-year-olds as part of an international AI Olympiad.
It’s impressive that they can solve competitions at such a young age.
They learn machine learning on their own.
How did you start teaching?

transcript.header: Transition to Teaching: From Competitor to Instructor

transcript.line: I joined a class at my university and was asked to teach instead of being a student.
So you wanted to join as a student but ended up teaching?
Yes, I was overqualified for the class.
Teaching helps you learn.
Absolutely. Teaching forces you to understand the material deeply.
How did your teaching journey continue?
I found teaching fulfilling and continued. I also realized I needed to improve my understanding of machine learning theory to teach effectively.
The best way to learn something is to teach it.
Totally agree.
When I studied machine learning, we focused on theory, but it wasn’t very practical.

transcript.header: Practical Curriculum Design: Production ML & MLOps

transcript.line: I prefer teaching practical skills, like production machine learning and MLOps.
How do you approach teaching now?
I design problems that students find interesting and build the curriculum around them. For example, I have a class where students build a classifier to detect bots in dialogues.
That’s a great approach.

transcript.header: Machine Learning System Design Projects & Real-World Work

transcript.line: Another class focuses on machine learning system design, where students work on real-world problems.
How did you develop your production machine learning skills?
After Kaggle, I worked as a data analyst and realized I needed to improve my Python and machine learning skills. I moved to Yandex, where I learned more about statistics and Python.
Later, I worked at Mechanica AI, where I learned about Docker, Kubernetes, and FastAPI. This helped me become a full-stack machine learning engineer.
It’s interesting how you and Mikhail took different paths but ended up in similar roles.
Yes, we started from different positions but ended up doing similar work.
How do you approach teaching now?

transcript.header: Problem-Centered Assignments: Bot Detection Case Study

transcript.line: I design problems that students find interesting and build the curriculum around them. For example, I have a class where students build a classifier to detect bots in dialogues.
Do students work individually or in teams?

transcript.header: Teamwork, Communication & Dual Leaderboards (ML + Technical)

transcript.line: They work in teams to learn collaboration and communication.
Where is the competitive aspect in your classes?
Students deploy their classifiers on a platform, and we have leaderboards for both ML metrics and technical metrics like uptime and response time.
That’s an amazing idea.
It helps students focus on building reliable solutions.
Do you have a leaderboard?
Yes, we have two leaderboards: one for ML metrics and one for technical metrics.
How many students are in your classes?
Around 80 students per class.
You also teach online courses, right?

transcript.header: Online Education at Scale: Coursera Course & 100k Students

transcript.line: Yes, I created a Coursera course on winning Kaggle competitions, which has been taken by over 100,000 students.
How do you manage teaching so many students online?
Online courses are a different format. You design the class, create automated checks, and have a team to answer questions.
Your approach to teaching is inspiring.
Thank you.
Do you develop the platform yourself?

transcript.header: Teaching Platform Development & Student-Built Software

transcript.line: No, I oversee the development, but students and mentors handle the coding.
Are students developing it, or is it professional software engineers?
Students develop it as part of a university project.
How do you manage the turnover of students?

transcript.header: Documentation, Mentorship & Industry Partnerships

transcript.line: We document everything and have mentors to guide new students.
Do you bring in industry mentors?
Yes, we have mentors from companies like Tinkoff.
Do you have a few more minutes for questions?
Of course.

transcript.header: Demonstrating Kaggle’s Business Value to Managers

transcript.line: One question is about convincing managers of the value of Kaggle.
It’s tricky, but showing examples of successful Kagglers in the company or industry can help.
Another question: Is there a secret trick that works in competitions?

transcript.header: Competition Essentials: EDA, Validation & No Single Trick

transcript.line: There’s no single trick, but careful data exploration and validation are key.
So the secret is to be thorough.
Exactly.

transcript.header: Generative AI & AutoML: Productivity vs. Winning Solutions

transcript.line: How does generative AI affect competitive machine learning?
Tools like ChatGPT can boost productivity, but they can’t replace the need for careful problem-solving.
Do people use autoML in competitions?
Yes, tools like AutoML can provide good baselines, but they can’t deliver winning solutions alone.

transcript.header: Career Reflections: Current Activity and Kaggle Legacy

transcript.line: What’s your current Kaggle rank?
It’s not great. I don’t compete actively anymore.
People still recognize you from your Kaggle days.
Yes, Kaggle was a big part of my career.
Do you still compete?
No, I focus on teaching now.
There are still people who make a living from Kaggle.
Yes, some people are still very active and successful.
The Kaggle leaderboard has changed a lot.
Yes, it’s a different landscape now.

transcript.header: Closing Remarks & Episode Wrap-Up

transcript.line: Alexander, thank you for joining us today. It was great to talk to you.
Thank you, Alexey. Thank you, everyone.
Have a great week!

description: Discover AI infrastructure strategies: open source orchestration, on-prem   economics and distributed training at scale to cut costs, boost performance and control.
short: Trends in AI Infrastructure
title: Post-ChatGPT AI Infrastructure: Open Source Orchestration, On-Prem Economics & Distributed Training at Scale

transcript.header: Episode Kickoff & Guest Introduction

transcript.line: This week, we'll talk about AI infrastructure and everything related to it. We might touch on trends in AI infrastructure, but we'll see where the conversation goes.

We have a special guest today: Andrey, the founder and CEO of DSec, which is an open-source alternative to Kubernetes and SLAM. I’m not sure what SLAM is, but we’ll probably talk about that. The idea behind DSec is to simplify the setup of AI infrastructure. Before DSec, Andrey worked at JetBrains for 10 years, helping different teams develop the best developer tools. Welcome, Andrey!
Thank you, Alexey, for the introduction and for inviting me. I'm excited to talk about infrastructure and everything related to it.
We've known each other for quite some time, so it was long overdue to invite you. Thanks for accepting the invitation.

As always, the questions for today's interview were prepared by Johanna Bayer. Thanks, Johanna, for your help. Let's start with the main topic: AI infrastructure. But before we dive into that, could you tell us about your career journey so far?

transcript.header: Career Background: JetBrains, DataSpell, and Move into AI

transcript.line: Sure. I started my professional career as a software engineer, though back then, I didn't even consider it a professional career—I just enjoyed coding. I even skipped school sometimes to work on coding problems.
You started coding in high school?
Yes, exactly. I miss those days when I coded just for fun.
Don’t we all miss those days?

After that, I switched to professional software development and worked in different companies. One of the companies I worked for was Experts, based in Saint Petersburg. They made professional tools for traders, like for options and stocks, and I really enjoyed it.
Then, I joined JetBrains, which was basically a dream job for me as a programmer. I know many others feel the same way about JetBrains tools. When I was invited to join, it was super exciting.

I spent 10 years there, working with different teams. I started with IntelliJ, then helped launch a data group, which is an IDE for working with databases. I also worked with other IDEs, including helping launch GoLand as a Go IDE. Eventually, I joined the PyCharm team as a product manager.

I was working on DataSpell, which is a dedicated IDE for data analysis and data science. It’s also part of PyCharm, and this is where I was first introduced to machine learning. That eventually led me to leave JetBrains and focus fully on this area.
How did you decide to focus on this technology? What made you choose this problem to solve full-time?

transcript.header: Origins of DStack: Reducing AI Infrastructure Cost of Ownership

transcript.line: That's a great question. There are a lot of factors, and it's certainly a topic we could discuss at length. But if I were to summarize a few specific reasons:

I remember, during my interviews with various ML teams, I often asked, "What’s standing in the way of your team?" There were many challenges, but one thing that stood out to me was that there are still two main ways to do machine learning: on-premises and in the cloud.

Some teams couldn't use either because of cost. On-prem infrastructure requires a large upfront investment, and you need to ensure you're fully utilizing the hardware, which can be difficult to predict. This makes it a risky decision for many companies.
On the other hand, cloud infrastructure is expensive, especially for cutting-edge AI development. Many companies are concerned about the cost.

The more I worked with different teams, the more I realized that there were ways to work around these issues. Tools like Terraform, Kubernetes, and Docker have made cloud development much more predictable and less complex. But the problem with costs still remains.
That’s why I thought there should be a solution that could greatly reduce the cost of ownership and simplify the process for everyone, which led me to start working on DSec.

transcript.header: Cloud vs On-Prem Costs and MLOps Limitations (SageMaker example)

transcript.line: Yes, there are existing tools for machine learning, like SageMaker, but as you mentioned, cost becomes a major issue.

SageMaker is a great counterexample. It’s one of the most mature MLOps platforms for working with AWS. However, it doesn’t address all the issues, which is why many people are hesitant to use cloud services in the first place.

I remember when I joined my previous company as a senior data scientist about six years ago. The first thing I wanted was a machine with GPUs, preferably with a couple of them. I wrote a proposal for this, and everyone approved it, but it never happened. The cost of ownership was too high—the machine had to be housed somewhere, and someone had to maintain it.

With the cloud, it’s often easier to just click a button, but then you get the bill a month later, and it’s much more expensive than expected. One of the first tasks I had as a senior data scientist was porting some code from SageMaker to Kubernetes. I guess that's how people used to manage it.

transcript.header: Cloud-to-On-Prem Realities in the Post-ChatGPT Era

transcript.line: Yes, and while many of these challenges are still relevant today, there are even bigger challenges ahead. The "ChatGPT moment" has introduced new issues, which makes AI infrastructure an even more important topic today.
How long have you been doing this?
It’s been about 2 years, maybe a bit more.
I think we've known each other for around 2 years, maybe a little longer. So, I’ve basically seen this start.
Yes, I was doing some experiments even while I was still at JetBrains. It became official when we did the first project with JetBrains.

So, the next question is: how did you begin working on AI infrastructure? But I think you've partly answered that already. You started at JetBrains, right? You saw things related to machine learning, realized there was a problem, and started working on it.

Yes, in a general sense. JetBrains is a very flat company where everyone has a dedicated role, but it’s close to programming. Many marketing people at JetBrains were originally programmers, which is how I got into marketing and product management. Everything at JetBrains revolves around developer tools, so your full-time job is to think about the developer experience—gathering feedback from the community, passing it to the development team, and spreading the word. For me, transitioning from JetBrains to AI infrastructure wasn’t a huge change. I was still working on developer tools, just focusing more specifically on AI infrastructure. My title might have changed, but not much else.
Well, now you have to figure out how to get funding yourself, right? Previously, it was different.
Especially working on open-source, yes.

transcript.header: Choosing Open Source: Developer Tools, Feedback, and Community

transcript.line: Speaking of open-source, why did you decide to work in the open? I see many companies starting as closed-source but eventually moving to open-source. Why did you choose to follow this model and make all your code open from the beginning?

I think it’s a clear pattern. Many developer tools are open-source, and while we don’t always know the exact reasons, there’s a pattern to it. Of course, companies have commercial interests, and not many are fully nonprofit. OpenAI, for example, started as a nonprofit, but that changed. In the end, the model reflects the best way to achieve the company’s goals. Sometimes the goal changes, or the way to achieve it changes, and that’s fine. I wouldn’t argue about whether being commercial or nonprofit is better. We see that most companies eventually go commercial, and many leverage open-source to move forward.

When we started, we weren’t sure if open-source was the right decision. But the more we talked to teams using different tools, the more we learned. One of the main benefits of open-source, especially in infrastructure, is that it allows early adopters to give feedback, which helps improve the tool. Open-source is one of the best frameworks for this process. There are other ways, but for me, as someone who’s always worked with developer tools, it’s easier to communicate directly with developers and understand their problems. Open-source fits well because I can relate to the development team.

transcript.header: Open vs Proprietary Models: Business Models and Trade-Offs

transcript.line: I don’t know the full story behind OpenAI either, but I think they initially released many things as open-source. GPT-2 was open-source, and they also released Whisper and CLIP. But when they released GPT-3, they realized it was a gold mine. They thought, maybe this is something we should keep closed, but then others started reproducing GPT-3 and matching its performance. Now, OpenAI releases something, and the open-source community tries to catch up. What’s your opinion on that? With closed-source solutions like OpenAI and GPT-3, which give great performance, versus open-source solutions, where you have many different models with various characteristics and use cases?

This is a big topic, and we could talk for hours about it. I’ve given talks on the comparison between closed-source and open-source models. It seems like many people are living in a bubble when they discuss which is better, proprietary or open-source. The world is much larger, and framing the question like that isn’t helpful. It’s not about what’s better; there are many factors to consider. It’s not even an important question to debate.
Okay, I’m just wondering where the industry is heading.

If you think about proprietary and open-source models, they represent two different types of businesses. Proprietary AI is a service, centralized with one company offering it. There are many engineers working on different aspects of that service, and AI, in this case, is not just a model—it’s a service that impacts all aspects of our lives.
Right, so GPT is much more than just a model.

transcript.header: Decentralization in AI: Privacy, Control, and Industry Fit

transcript.line: Yes, it’s more than just the model. It’s like a new version of Google. Google changed our lives because we can search for anything. Now, GPT is changing how we work, not just how we search. It’s a disruptive change.

Open-source AI is a different business. It’s decentralized, where various companies and stakeholders contribute to different aspects. For example, in banking, privacy and control are essential, and a monolithic AI model doesn’t fit. Open-source allows companies to protect their privacy and control. It’s also about competition. If businesses don’t protect their margins, they won’t be able to compete. Open-source AI is important because it allows companies to maintain their competitive edge. Whether open-source AI is better than GPT-3 doesn’t matter as much. It’s about the approach that fits the business model.
So, it depends on the use case.

Yes, the whole point here is decentralization. Open source is about decentralization, and it’s a mega trend that isn’t influenced by quality. The quality is a result of this mega trend. We see that open source models are better. It's not that people use open source models because they are better than GPT models; they are better because people need them.
But it's not that they are better in terms of performance; they are better in other aspects, like being able to control the data flow or hosting them yourself.

Yes, and that's when we can compare some aspects of models. But to me, it doesn’t make sense to compare them side by side. What makes sense for open source models is whether they are customizable, and that’s why we use them—they are easy to customize. What's even more important is that it’s becoming less of a "rocket science" process. The process of retraining and post-training is getting easier and simpler because of decentralization. Whether we like it or not, this trend is here, and we can’t influence it.

Do you know if big companies, like Meta, contribute a lot to the open source community, especially in AI, with models like LLaMA? Do they publicly share information on how exactly they train their models and what their AI infrastructure is?

I want to answer for sure, but I’d say yes. Typically, this is shared in a technical report. Even OpenAI, while not open-sourcing most of what they do, still shares some information on how they contribute to the community. This started even before, for example, with the "Attention is All You Need" paper from 2017. Even though it wasn’t open source, the paper on the transformer algorithm was. And then Meta went further, for example, with the LLaMA model. They made the weights available with LLaMA 3.1. Some people argue whether "open source" applies to models, and some prefer to say "open weights." To be honest, I’m not that picky.

Even OpenAI shared a lot of details about their post-training and pre-training processes. LLaMA also released a technical report on how they trained their models, providing a lot of details on the training process. This is also how the community learns.

This is a good example of decentralization—it’s not just about the morals, it’s about sharing technical details on how training and post-training were done, how many GPUs were used, and the architecture of the model. A lot of details are publicly available, and this is one of the best ways to learn.

Some might think technical reports are boring, but I personally encourage everyone to read them. They are actually very interesting. I’m a big fan of books, and while I used to read a lot of fiction, I now find reading fiction less exciting. I actually find technical reports much more entertaining.

Since you find these reports entertaining, I’m curious—what challenges do these companies face, and do these challenges also apply to smaller companies? Larger companies like Meta, Google, and OpenAI have different challenges from smaller ones, right? What are these challenges in general, and how do they affect trends in AI infrastructure?

I consider myself a generalist, so I’m interested not only in the technical side of things but also in other aspects. When you ask about challenges, there are technical challenges in every team, whether it's an infrastructure team, an AI team, or a data team.

transcript.header: Training at Scale: GPU Requirements and Distributed Challenges

transcript.line: Since we’re talking about AI infrastructure, let’s focus on that. To train a model, we need thousands of GPUs. How do we get them in the first place? How do we coordinate this? These are all questions we need to consider when starting such a project.

Yes, we need to think not only about technical problems but also financial ones. We know for sure that without GPUs, we can’t train models. For example, LLaMA 3.1 was trained using 16,000 GPUs. To put that into perspective, Meta likely has an order of magnitude more GPUs in total. If they used only a small fraction of what they have, they could train LLaMA 3.1.

The first challenge is infrastructure. However, I want to mention that while GPUs and money are important, they are not everything. There are other factors to consider. For instance, DeepSig recently released a V3 model in December. They used only a small fraction of what Meta used to train LLaMA 3.1, yet they trained a model that is significantly better in terms of benchmarks.
I’ve seen posts about this in my social media feeds just a few days ago.

Yes, DeepSig’s release happened at the end of December. They trained a model with a fraction of Meta’s resources, and the model performed significantly better in benchmarks compared to LLaMA 3.1. What I’m trying to say is that while GPUs and money are important, they are not the only factors.

But back to your question—retraining is a large-scale task involving many GPUs, and it’s distributed. Distributed training is challenging. If you speak to people working in this area, they will tell you how complex the process is. When you have tons of GPUs, you need to coordinate everything. If something goes wrong on one of the nodes, you have to deal with it.
The more GPUs you have, the higher the chances something will go wrong, right?
Yes, and you need to manage that at scale. There are many other issues to address, but handling this one is a major challenge.

Do you know what this actually looks like? There’s probably a computer with 4 or 8 GPUs, another one with 4 or 8 GPUs, and all these computers are part of a network. You need to distribute the training process across all these machines, where each computer has several GPUs, and each GPU needs to compute something and then send the weights or gradients back to a central location. Is this roughly how it works?
